analysis.one_liner: Let Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers like the VA does.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices and give beneficiaries federal-discount prices died in committee, with no vote and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let every Medicare beneficiary buy prescription drugs at the Federal Supply Schedule — the discounted prices the federal government already pays when agencies like the VA buy in bulk. It also would have repealed the "noninterference" clause in the Medicare drug law, which bans the government from negotiating prices with drug makers, and given the Health and Human Services Secretary the same bargaining power the VA and Defense Department have. The goal was for seniors to pay the lowest possible price for their medications.
analysis.who_benefits: All Medicare beneficiaries — seniors and people with disabilities on Medicare — who would have been eligible to buy their prescriptions at the lower prices the federal government already pays, and who would have benefited from the Secretary of HHS negotiating directly with drug manufacturers on their behalf [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every person eligible for Medicare Part A or enrolled in Part B could have obtained prescription drugs at Federal Supply Schedule prices — the discounted rates the federal government pays for drugs it buys in bulk.

The bill repealed the 'noninterference' provision that bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in negotiations between drug manufacturers, pharmacies, and prescription drug plans, or from requiring a formulary to adopt a price structure.

It gave the HHS Secretary negotiating authority like that of the VA and Defense Department, whose bulk purchasing power gets steep discounts, with the stated purpose of ensuring beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would have had to negotiate lower prices for Medicare's business instead of selling through private plans at whatever prices the market bears. HHS would also have taken on the administrative cost of running negotiations.

drawbacks.text: The bill directed the Secretary to push for the 'lowest possible price,' and price negotiation tools like formulary control can mean narrower coverage choices; beneficiaries could have faced trade-offs between lower prices and access to some newer or brand-name drugs.

Drug manufacturers and their allies argued that government negotiation amounts to price-setting that could reduce investment in new medicines — a standard objection to letting Medicare bargain like the VA does, though the bill's supporters saw bulk-buying discounts as savings seniors were being denied.

The bill was one page with no co-sponsors and no committee action, so it never received the scrutiny — cost estimates, implementation details, how FSS access would work alongside private Part D plans — that a working bill needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was large: Medicare is one of the biggest drug purchasers in the world, and the bill would have let it bargain for prices the VA and other agencies already get, while letting beneficiaries buy at those federal rates directly. The main cost would fall on drug manufacturers, and the main design risk is that aggressive price-seeking can narrow drug choices. The bigger practical weakness is that the bill was a statement of principle — a single page, no cosponsors, never worked in committee — so it was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2005, referred to two committees and then a subcommittee, and nobody ever brought it up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the bill on December 22, 2005, right as the new Medicare Part D drug benefit was taking effect under a law that explicitly barred the government from negotiating drug prices.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and in early January 2006 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors; it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the noninterference ban stayed in place, Medicare kept buying through private plans without government price negotiation, and seniors kept paying prices set without federal bargaining power.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers kept un-negotiated Medicare prices

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give Medicare beneficiaries Federal Supply Schedule drug prices and authorize government price negotiation, and pursued no cosponsors before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (chair Joe Barton)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup after the bill was referred and sent to its Health Subcommittee; no further action appears in the record.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (chair Bill Thomas)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on the day of introduction.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry with a stake in the noninterference clause
against.what_they_did: Supported keeping the Medicare drug law's ban on government price negotiation, which the bill would have repealed; outside the chamber, this position was widely reported during the Part D debates.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, so no party split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to negotiate prices with the federal government, using the same bulk-purchasing leverage the VA uses to get steep discounts, instead of selling into Medicare through private plans at un-negotiated prices. Repealing the noninterference clause removed a legal protection the industry had written into the Part D law.

industries.industry: Private Part D prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: The bill struck the provision barring HHS from interfering with plan–manufacturer negotiations and from dictating formulary price structures, so plans would have lost autonomy over pricing arrangements. They would have kept their role as the delivery channel for the drug benefit, but under federal negotiating authority they could not block.
